Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Data Storage & External Services

The photos table stores UUID identifiers, original filenames, MIME types, byte sizes, upload timestamps, dimensions and image bytes mapped with JPA @Lob. Upload and retrieval paths use the database, not a filesystem upload store. Compose configures Oracle XE and the oracle_data volume; the default local datasource targets Oracle on localhost, while the Docker profile targets oracle-db. Both profiles configure spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create, so schema recreation at application startup can remove existing photo data despite persistent database files. Database and administrator secrets are supplied through external configuration; no credential values are reproduced here.

Browser templates load Bootstrap CSS/JavaScript from jsDelivr. No application-level cache, broker, object-storage service or outbound business API integration was identified in the inspected source. H2 is declared only as a test-scoped dependency, not the configured production store.

Evidence: Photo.java, PhotoServiceImpl.java, application property files and Compose cited above.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Layered monolith with constructor injection: MVC controllers depend on the PhotoService interface; its transactional implementation depends on a Spring Data repository. Reads use read-only transaction annotations.
  • Database-centric image storage: binaries and metadata share the same entity/table. Gallery and navigation queries explicitly use Oracle constructs including NVL, ROWNUM, SYSDATE and DUAL, coupling persistence to Oracle.
  • Public browsing, protected mutations: SecurityConfig requires authentication for POST /upload and /detail/*/delete, permits other requests, disables CSRF and uses stateless HTTP Basic with a BCrypt-encoded, externally configured in-memory administrator. No application TLS configuration was identified.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicit HTTP endpoints provide gallery HTML, multipart upload with JSON results, photo detail HTML, deletion redirects, and binary image delivery. Requests use synchronous controller-to-service calls; browser upload uses asynchronous JavaScript fetch but is not a messaging or background-job contract.

Paths are unversioned; no header/query-based versioning is implemented. Controller names below all belong to photoalbum-java-app. Status codes describe explicit controller behavior plus the configured authentication boundary; they are not a guarantee of uniform framework error bodies.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:18-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:23-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:46-59; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:97-131,176-179.

Upload response contract. The completed batch envelope contains success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads. success is true only when at least one uploaded photo has been reloaded into the result list. Successful entries are controller-created metadata projections, not serialized Photo entities; failed entries contain fileName and error. Empty-list/handled multipart errors instead return success:false with error:"No files provided". Clients must inspect the envelope even on HTTP 200; an all-failed batch still returns 200. A successful upload whose subsequent lookup returns empty is omitted from both lists. Exceptions from that subsequent lookup are not caught by the upload handler, so the batch JSON envelope is not guaranteed on unexpected failures. A missing required files parameter is a framework binding error, not explicitly normalized by this handler. Multipart request/file-size limits affect acceptance; see configuration-inventory.md for settings and business-workflows.md for validation details.

Binary response contract. Image responses set Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size. No content-disposition/download contract or JSON image payload is defined (PhotoFileController.java:74-86).

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous application flow: Controllers invoke PhotoService / PhotoServiceImpl directly; the service invokes PhotoRepository synchronously through JPA/JDBC. The database is the only identified backend service dependency. Browser JavaScript sends a same-origin multipart POST and uses returned metadata to construct photo/detail links (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:90-131,155-179).
  • No async backend messaging: No broker clients, events, queue consumers, pub/sub contracts, or background upload acknowledgment/polling endpoint were found in application source or dependencies.
  • Resilience and failures: No explicit application retry policy, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback backend, REST client timeout, or JDBC query/connect timeout is configured in inspected application files. Do not interpret that as infinite timeouts: driver/framework defaults remain unspecified here. Gallery retrieval failure renders an empty list; detail failure redirects home; deletion failure sets an error flash attribute and redirects; binary retrieval failure returns 500. Upload failures are usually per-file results, not automatic retries (HomeController.java:40-49,69-107; DetailController.java:38-78; PhotoFileController.java:44-86; PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-184). Container restart-on-failure is process lifecycle behavior, not an HTTP retry policy (docker-compose.yml:46).
  • Discovery and routing: No Eureka, Consul, service registry, client-side load balancer, or API gateway is present. Compose uses the oracle-db hostname for JDBC connectivity; standalone defaults use localhost. There is no multi-backend gateway aggregation; upload batch aggregation combines local per-file outcomes.
  • Availability: Compose orders the application after database health. Required database/admin credentials must be supplied for configured startup. See configuration-inventory.md for the startup/configuration chain; no credential values are reproduced here (docker-compose.yml:32-43; SecurityConfig.java:33-42).
  • Authentication and authorization: Spring Security uses stateless HTTP Basic. POST /upload and /detail/*/delete require authentication; other requests are permitted. An in-memory user is assigned an ADMIN role, but the route rules check only authentication, not role/ownership. No JWT, OAuth2, method-level authorization, or form-login endpoint is configured. CSRF is explicitly disabled (SecurityConfig.java:28-59).
  • Transport: No HTTPS listener, TLS termination proxy, or explicit JDBC TLS configuration was found in the supplied runtime configuration. The application publishes HTTP 8080. External TLS termination cannot be established from this repository; HTTP Basic therefore requires deployment-level transport protection not evidenced here.
  • Browser authentication UX: Upload JavaScript supplies no explicit Authorization header or login flow and reports non-2xx upload responses generically. Browser-managed previously established Basic credentials may still be used; authenticated mutations remain an API requirement (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:102-131; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-51).

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose resolves required secret inputs before starting containers; missing/empty required values fail interpolation (docker-compose.yml:7,10,36,38).
  2. oracle-db → Oracle initialization and mounted startup scripts. Both shell scripts require ORACLE_PWD and APP_USER_PASSWORD; create-user.sh:15-17 additionally sleeps 30 seconds. Scripts create the configured application user if absent; the numbered script also applies grants to an existing user.
  3. photoalbum-java-app → waits for → oracle-db, using Compose depends_on: condition: service_healthy (docker-compose.yml:41-43). The check invokes SQL*Plus with the application credentials against local Oracle XE and issues a simple query; interval 30 seconds, timeout 10 seconds, retries 15, start period 180 seconds (docker-compose.yml:19-24).
  4. Application startup requires the datasource configuration and app.admin.password resolution. Application restart policy is on-failure; no application container health check, custom startup timeout, readiness probe, config-server retry, or discovery dependency is declared.

The Oracle shell scripts do not explicitly enable SQLPlus WHENEVER SQLERROR EXIT, and the Compose check relies on the SQLPlus process exit status. These configured checks therefore should not be represented as proof that all SQL failures reliably block readiness. No running-service readiness was verified.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  1. Operator copies .env.example to ignored .env and supplies unique passwords, or exports equivalent shell variables (.env.example:1-17; .gitignore:201-204). All sample passwords are deliberately omitted here.
  2. Compose checks required values and maps the Oracle administrator password to ORACLE_PWD; the schema password is shared between Oracle startup scripts and Spring datasource configuration.
  3. Oracle scripts authenticate as SYSTEM, create the configured schema user when absent, and grant database privileges. This is password-based database administration, not cloud identity or secret-vault provisioning (oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:19-43).
  4. Application receives the schema credential and independent admin credential. SecurityConfig.java:28-42 BCrypt-encodes the configured admin password into an in-memory user store; this is not encryption of the source .env or container environment.
  5. Test resources supply separate test-only settings with masked credentials. No automated rotation or secret retrieval pipeline is evidenced. README Azure Key Vault/managed identity examples are prospective instructions, not implemented secret flows.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared collection of photographs and view individual images with chronological navigation. Authenticated operators can add photographs in batches and permanently remove them.

Evidence below refers to repository-relative source paths and line numbers. This document describes implemented behavior, not proposed features; no credential values are reproduced.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo collection managementA photograph retained with its original name, image content, upload information, and optional dimensions for presentation.Independent collection item; previous and next photographs are determined by upload time, not explicit relationships. No album, owner, or user association is modeled.
UploadResult (operation outcome, not a persisted entity)PhotoService / Photo ingestionCommunicates whether one attempted upload succeeded, its resulting photo reference, or a failure explanation.Links a successful attempt to a Photo; the controller groups outcomes across the submitted batch.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:12-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:3-14; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:212-230.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application with one business service, not a microservice topology. Context names below describe responsibilities rather than independently deployed services.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService, implemented by PhotoServiceImplShared photo collection: ingestion, retrieval, chronological navigation, removalPhoto; produces UploadResultPhotoRepository and its configured database; image-header readers for optional dimensions
HomeController (entry-point adapter)Gallery presentation and batch upload coordinationNone; composes Photo metadata and upload outcomesPhotoService
DetailController (entry-point adapter)Individual-photo viewing and removal feedbackNonePhotoService
PhotoFileController (entry-point adapter)Delivery of stored image contentNonePhotoService

PhotoRepository-backed storage is the source of truth for both image content and collection metadata. Controllers share the same service; no separate domain exchanges identifiers over a backend network API. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-46,154-169,190-209; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-29; controller constructors at HomeController.java:29-33, DetailController.java:23-27, and PhotoFileController.java:28-32 under src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Add a batch of photographs

  1. A user selects or drops files into the gallery. The browser applies Client upload screening, then submits eligible files to POST /upload; authentication is required before the controller is reached.
  2. HomeController applies Batch presence, then processes the files sequentially through PhotoService. Each file has its own service invocation rather than a single batch-wide business transaction.
  3. PhotoService applies Server upload eligibility and Image dimension ceiling, reads image bytes, and attempts optional dimension extraction. Unavailable image readers or non-I/O dimension-extraction exceptions can leave dimensions absent.
  4. For an accepted file, the service creates a Photo, assigns its identity and upload time, and saves the content and metadata together. A rejection or caught read/save error produces a failed UploadResult instead.
  5. After a successful service result, HomeController looks the Photo up again to construct the display metadata. It builds separate successful-photo and failed-upload lists and applies Batch outcome.
  6. The browser reports returned outcomes and prepends successful photographs to the gallery without a full reload. Images are fetched separately from their photo-content entry points.

This supports partial success: one rejected file does not deliberately cancel previously saved files. A successful save whose follow-up lookup returns no record is omitted from both result lists; a follow-up lookup exception is not caught by this upload controller.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-131,135-179; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:45-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-184; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:78-91.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and navigate individual photos

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController loads collection records through PhotoService and renders the gallery under Collection ordering.
  2. If collection retrieval throws, the controller logs the failure and renders an empty collection. The template's “No photos yet” message therefore also appears when retrieval failed; this is not evidence that the stored collection is empty.
  3. Opening GET /detail/{id} loads the requested Photo and obtains older and newer navigation candidates using Chronological navigation.
  4. The detail page combines the current Photo with neighboring identifiers. Missing neighbors suppress the corresponding navigation controls. An invalid, missing, or unsuccessfully loaded detail redirects to the gallery.
  5. Gallery and detail images initiate separate GET /photo/{id} requests. PhotoFileController retrieves stored bytes and applies Content availability. Successful delivery uses the recorded media type and disables browser caching, favoring fresh content.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-87; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:52-74,215-230; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:81-113; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-94.

Workflow 3: Permanently remove a photograph

  1. The detail page asks for browser confirmation before submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete. Authentication is required; the browser confirmation is not a server-side business safeguard.
  2. PhotoService looks up the Photo. If absent, it returns false; otherwise it deletes the stored Photo, including its image content, through PhotoRepository.
  3. DetailController redirects to the gallery with success, not-found, or caught-error feedback. No soft-delete state, restoration workflow, or compensating action is implemented.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:53-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-209; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78.

No scheduled business jobs, backend event listeners, messaging consumers, or business-data initialization runners were identified in src/main/java. The application entry point only starts the application (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14).

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no backend service-to-service aggregation calls, events, sagas, circuit breakers, or remote-service fallbacks in the traced implementation. Composition occurs inside the application:

  • Upload composition: one UploadResult per file is joined to a saved Photo by photo ID; the controller returns presentation metadata and grouped failures. Image bytes are not part of that upload response.
  • Detail composition: the current Photo's upload time drives two repository queries; their first results supply older/newer identifiers to the same view.
  • Content delivery: the browser uses the photo ID from gallery/detail metadata to request the stored image separately. Both metadata and bytes originate from the same Photo storage, not separate services.
  • Degradation: gallery retrieval errors render an empty gallery; detail failures redirect home; missing image content returns not-found, while caught image-serving errors return a server error. No alternative image store or placeholder fallback is implemented by the content controller.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50,69-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-57; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:215-230; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:172-185.

Business Workflow Sequence

Primary process: authenticated batch ingestion followed by gallery display. The alternatives represent actual local validation/error paths, not an unimplemented circuit-breaker mechanism.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation and decisions

RuleImplemented behaviorEvidence
Client upload screeningBrowser accepts JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP MIME types and files up to 10 MiB. It sends eligible files even if other selected files fail screening; it does not explicitly reject zero-length files.src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-87
Batch presenceNull/empty batch returns a bad-request result. The multipart exception handler also reports “No files provided,” without distinguishing other multipart failures.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:63-67,100-107
Server upload eligibilityLowercased submitted content type must be in the configured allowlist; size must be positive and no greater than the configured maximum. Supplied defaults allow the four image MIME types and 10 MiB per file; multipart settings also cap the whole request at 50 MB. A missing content type falls into the service's generic error handling, not a specific eligibility message.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:85-109,178-181; src/main/resources/application.properties:24-30
Image dimension ceilingWhen an image reader is available, header width multiplied by height must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels. An I/O exception rejects the upload; other extraction exceptions or no reader allow processing without dimensions. This is not a requirement that every accepted payload fully decode as an image.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:33-34,116-152
Photo metadata constraintsPhoto declares a nonblank original filename of at most 255 characters, positive/non-null size, nonblank MIME type of at most 50 characters, and non-null upload time. These are entity validation declarations, not explicit controller validation steps.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:28-64
Batch outcomeA processed batch returns an OK response even if all per-file uploads fail. Its success flag is true only when the successful-photo response list is nonempty. The configured maximum-files-per-upload value of 10 is not referenced by the traced controller/service or browser code and should not be treated as an enforced count limit.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:69-97; src/main/resources/application.properties:30; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-106
Collection orderingFull collection is newest-first by upload time. No filename deduplication or content-based duplicate detection is implemented in ingestion.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-29; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:154-169
Chronological navigationPrevious selects the first older result, ordered newest-first and capped at ten candidates. Next selects the first newer result, ordered oldest-first and restricted to database current time. Strict time comparisons exclude equal-timestamp peers; no ID tie-breaker is specified.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:37-62; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:215-230
Content availabilityBlank IDs, absent Photo records, or null/empty image bytes return not-found. Caught delivery exceptions return a server error.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:38-86

Lifecycle, consistency, and cross-cutting behavior

  • Lifecycle and computed information: accepted input becomes a saved Photo with a generated identity and local upload time; deletion removes it. Rejected attempts are not stored as business entities. There is no approval/publication state machine. Dimensions are derived from image headers; display sizes and dates are formatted by the views. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:78-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:116-169,190-205; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:104-130.
  • Transaction boundaries: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level transactions; read methods explicitly use read-only transactions. Controllers do not establish a batch-wide transaction. A successful save call is not itself proof that transaction commit will succeed: commit-time failures can escape after the service's internal catch blocks. Detail composition also uses separate service calls rather than one declared snapshot transaction. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,52-74,165-184,215-230; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:69-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-49.
  • Authorization: gallery, detail, and content reads are public. Upload and delete POST requests require authentication using stateless HTTP Basic. The configured account is assigned ADMIN, but endpoint rules check authentication rather than an ADMIN role or Photo ownership. No per-user collection isolation exists in the Photo model. CSRF protection is disabled in this configuration. Credential values are intentionally omitted. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-91.
  • Errors and audit: ingestion returns operation-level failures for caught validation/read/save errors; retrieval and deletion wrap storage exceptions in generic runtime exceptions. Controllers provide workflow-specific degradation described above. Logging records uploads, rejections, deletions, and retrieval/delivery failures; the content controller also logs filenames and a prefix of stored bytes. No persisted business audit trail, automatic retry, dead-letter flow, or compensating operation is implemented in the traced code. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:55-74,85-109,144-181,190-209; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The project targets Java 21 and inherits Spring Boot 3.5.0 (pom.xml:8–13,23–28). Framework upgrades should preserve alignment with the inherited dependency management. Commons IO is explicitly pinned to 2.14.0, so parent upgrades will not automatically update that declaration. Oracle driver compatibility with Java 21 and the target Oracle database must be checked against its effective managed version; the ojdbc8 artifact name alone does not establish incompatibility. No lifecycle lookup or vulnerability assessment was performed, so no end-of-life or CVE status is asserted.

Notable Observations

  • Only one recognized build/package manifest was found, the root pom.xml; it declares no Maven modules. No dependency lockfile was found, limiting transitive-version evidence.
  • DevTools is explicitly optional, not test-scoped (pom.xml:95–100); it is therefore counted among non-test declarations, without assuming production packaging behavior.
  • The comment above spring-boot-starter-json says “Image processing,” but the declared artifact is the JSON starter (pom.xml:75–79); no dedicated image-processing library is declared.
  • org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-maven-plugin is declared without a local version (pom.xml:103–110). It is build tooling, excluded from the library diagram and counts. No standalone logging, messaging, caching, or observability dependency is declared; this does not establish their absence transitively.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, persisted through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate to Oracle, with H2 used by the test profile. Photo bytes and metadata reside in the same database row; there is no mapped album or user entity.

No explicit version/optimistic-lock field, soft-delete flag, tenant/owner key, cascade mapping, or bidirectional relationship exists in this entity. No explicit lazy-fetch override is declared for its binary LOB.

PhotoServiceImpl has class-level @Transactional; retrieval and navigation methods override it with read-only transactions (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,52-70,215-229). Upload and deletion use the class-level transaction boundary. Metadata and bytes are saved together as one entity, not coordinated with an external object store.

Key Repository Methods

ServiceRepositoryNotable MethodsPurpose
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Native SQL reads all rows, including binary data, newest first; Oracle NVL supplies a fallback MIME type. No pagination parameter.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedBefore(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Parameterized native SQL selects strictly older rows ordered newest first, capped at ten using Oracle ROWNUM.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedAfter(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Parameterized native SQL selects strictly newer rows up to Oracle SYSDATE, ordered oldest first; uses DUAL and has no explicit row cap.

Interface and SQL source: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-62. It extends JpaRepository and inherits standard CRUD and paging operations. The service uses inherited lookup/save/delete operations, but these are not custom queries. No custom bulk aggregation finder, derived finder, stored-procedure invocation, or separate metadata projection was found. All three native queries select photo_data, so gallery/navigation reads also retrieve image payloads.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application persistence boundary uses one datasource and one mapped table. All observed photo reads/writes go through PhotoServiceImpl and PhotoRepository; no database-per-service topology, cross-service database reads, remote data aggregation, outbox, or separate CQRS read store is present in the inspected code. Read-only transaction annotations separate read intent, not data ownership or physical storage.

Photo payloads are authoritative database LOBs, not filesystem paths. Upload reads file bytes and persists them with the metadata (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:111-166); file delivery reads those bytes from the entity (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:46-69). A checked-in image exists under src/main/resources/static/uploads/, but the current persistence model contains no filesystem-reference field; that asset is not evidence of a separate active upload datastore.

No persisted user/album ownership relation or row-level tenant boundary is modeled. Authentication uses an in-memory administrator rather than a user table (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-42). Database bootstrap grants schema-object privileges rather than DBA access (oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:31-43); this is a database-account boundary, not per-photo authorization.
